criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p athena-core rebase_job_branch`. A test against a bare origin has two jobs stacked locally, with main moved after the second was verified. rebase_job_branch (taking git, the state dir and the remote as arguments) leaves the second job's landing commit rebased onto origin's main, and `git log` shows a linear history. A second case, a conflict in the job's own commit, leaves origin's main and the local branch unchanged.
criteria.evidence: Ran it: 4 tests passed. rebase_job_branch_lands_second_job_on_the_moved_main sets up a bare origin and pushes an outside commit from a second clone. It then asserts the following. The outside commit is an ancestor of the landed commit. `rev-list --merges` over the range is empty, and each of the 2 new commits has one parent. The log subjects are job B then job A. The bare main is unchanged, so nothing was pushed. A second run gives Current. rebase_job_branch_conflict_changes_nothing asserts that HEAD still equals the old commit and the bare main still equals the outside commit. Two more tests cover the Unchecked cases: origin unreachable, and a published head.

findings.summary: Commits stacked above the job's landing commit are also turned into records-only commits when they conflict, but the CHANGELOG and design doc only talk about an "earlier" commit.
findings.evidence: plan_rebase replays every first-parent commit from the fork up to `head`, not just up to `landed`. Any commit other than `landed` that conflicts goes through commit_with_records. If a later-stacked job is still queued, its code is silently dropped from the branch, and that job will later be held. The rustdoc says "any other commit", but the user-facing docs say "earlier". A later-stacked commit can exist because queue order is not stacking order.
findings.location: crates/athena-core/src/gh/landing.rs plan_rebase (the `None =>` arm); CHANGELOG.md; docs/design/async-drain.md section 6

findings.summary: If the job's own commit replays to an empty change, the result reports the previous commit as the landed one.
findings.evidence: When merge_tree returns a tree equal to tip's tree, no commit is made, and `new_landed = tip`. That is the commit below, which can be another job's commit or main itself. This happens when main already holds the job's changes, for example after a cherry-pick. The result is then Moved with a `landed` that does not carry this job's trailers. land_pr's merged-content check is the backstop. Returning Current in this case, or treating it as an error, would be clearer.
findings.location: crates/athena-core/src/gh/landing.rs plan_rebase, `Some(tree)` arm then `if commit == landed`

findings.summary: The linear-history check uses `rev-list --merges` and a parent count instead of `git log`.
findings.evidence: The criterion says "`git log` shows a linear history". The test checks the same property directly: no merges in the range, and one parent per commit. It also reads the subjects with `git log --format=%s`.

summary:
The candidate passes. It adds `Rebase`, `plan_rebase` and `rebase_job_branch` in athena-core's gh/landing.rs and re-exports them from gh/mod.rs. It also adds a CHANGELOG entry and a note in section 6 of async-drain.md. I ran the targeted tests on this snapshot: 7 plan_rebase tests and 4 rebase_job_branch tests passed, and the full athena-core suite passed (799 passed, 1 ignored). The tests use real repositories and a real bare origin, with no mocks. They cover all of these:
- a clean move onto a moved main
- a branch that is already current
- a conflict in the job's own commit, which holds the job back
- an earlier conflicting commit carried as records only, where the production Records::load still loads the held-back job's candidate, verification and outcome
- a clean earlier commit that rides along
- a linear rebase of the second job onto a moved bare main, with nothing pushed
- a conflict that leaves both the local branch and origin's main unchanged

Athena's recorded fmt, clippy and test results are green. The diff touches exactly the four expected files, and drain.rs and the existing tests are untouched. Both docs say that clean earlier commits ride along, that the re-check rule does not cover stacked content, that a conflicting earlier commit is kept as records only, and that the drain wiring is a follow-up. The user accepted the reading that cut the drain wiring, so the missing drain test is not a mismatch. The records-only carry is sound: it applies only the commit's own records/ changes onto the new tip, using commit_with_records and a three-way merge-tree. Two minor findings remain. First, conflicting commits stacked above the job's own commit are also reduced to records only, but the docs only mention earlier commits. Second, if the job's own commit replays to an empty change, the previous commit is reported as the landed one.
